title: Motorcycle Accident Lawyer Cost: Contingency Fees and Case Costs (2026)
description: What a motorcycle accident lawyer charges, why rider cases cost more to build, how shared fault cuts your net, and what to ask before signing.
h1: How much does a motorcycle accident lawyer cost?
summary: Motorcycle accident lawyers almost always work on contingency: a percentage of the recovery, commonly quoted at one-third, and nothing if there is no recovery. Some states cap fees (Michigan at one-third; Connecticut and Florida on sliding scales). Rider cases often cost more to build because fault and helmet questions are disputed, and your net also depends on shared-fault reductions, case costs and medical liens.
body:
How motorcycle accident lawyers charge

Motorcycle injury cases are handled like other personal injury claims: almost always on a contingency fee, a percentage of what is recovered, with no fee if nothing is recovered. Your agreement must be written and signed, must list the percentage at each stage (settlement, trial, appeal), and must say whether case expenses are deducted before or after the percentage is calculated.[1] One-third is the most commonly quoted starting point; it is the legal maximum in Michigan injury cases,[2] and Florida presumes fees above 33⅓% of the first $1 million excessive if a case settles before the defendant answers (40% after an answer).[3] Connecticut caps injury fees on a sliding scale starting at 33⅓% of the first $300,000.[4]

The percentage on a motorcycle case is rarely different from a car case at the same firm. What differs is how much work and money the case needs, which shows up in costs and in whether the firm will accept the case at all.

What makes rider cases more expensive to bring

  • Disputed fault. Insurers often argue the rider was speeding, lane-splitting or not visible. Answering that may need scene photos, vehicle inspections, helmet-camera footage, phone records or an accident reconstructionist, all of which are case costs.
  • Injury severity. Riders have little protection, so cases more often involve surgery, long treatment and future-care evidence, which means more records and expert opinions.
  • Helmet questions. Helmet rules vary widely. As of October 2026, IIHS lists 17 states plus DC that require helmets for all riders, 30 states with partial laws (usually by age), and 3 states with no helmet law: Illinois, Iowa and New Hampshire.[5] Whether not wearing a helmet can reduce damages depends on your state's law and the injury involved, so it can add expert work on causation.
  • Gear and bike value. Custom parts, aftermarket equipment and riding gear may need documentation to be paid at full value.
  • Limited insurance. If the at-fault driver carries only state-minimum liability coverage, your own uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage may matter as much as the lawsuit. Ask whether the fee applies to a UM/UIM claim on your own policy and at what rate.

How shared fault changes your net

In many states a rider who is partly at fault can still recover, but damages are reduced by the rider's share of fault, and some states bar recovery once the rider's share reaches a set threshold. The rules differ by state, so treat the example below as arithmetic, not a rule for your case.

Illustrative example only. Total agreed damages are $80,000, and the rider is found 25% at fault. Recovery: $80,000 × (1 − 0.25) = $60,000. Fee at one-third of the gross: $60,000 × 1/3 = $20,000. Case costs: $4,500. Health plan reimbursement: $7,000. Net to the rider: $60,000 − $20,000 − $4,500 − $7,000 = $28,500.

If the same agreement takes the fee after costs: ($60,000 − $4,500) × 1/3 = $18,500, and the net becomes $60,000 − $18,500 − $4,500 − $7,000 = $30,000.

Health-plan and Medicare reimbursement rules can reduce what the payer takes back; Medicare, for example, reduces its recovery by its proportional share of fees and costs.[6] See the personal injury lawyer cost page for a full lien example and the general deadline for every state.

When hourly help makes sense

If your injuries were minor and you only need someone to review an insurer's offer or a release, some lawyers will do a limited-scope review by the hour instead of taking a share of the claim. Clio puts the national average lawyer rate at $349 an hour in its 2025 data.[7] Example: 3 hours × $349 = $1,047 for a document review, compared with a one-third fee on a $9,000 offer: $9,000 × 1/3 = $3,000. For a larger or disputed claim, contingency usually makes more sense because the lawyer carries the risk. See hourly vs. flat fees.

Case costs you may see on the settlement statement

These are typically advanced by the firm and repaid from the recovery. Prices vary by provider and region, so ask for actual invoices rather than estimates.

Common case cost items in a motorcycle injury claim
Cost itemWhen it appearsQuestion to ask
Police report, medical records and billsAlmost every claimAre copy charges passed through at cost?
Bike and helmet inspection or storageDisputed fault or product defectWho chose the inspector, and is storage billed monthly?
Accident reconstruction expertSpeed, lane position or visibility disputedWill you ask me before hiring an expert?
Medical expert or life-care plannerSurgery, permanent injury or future careIs the expert needed before suit, or only for trial?
Court filing, service and deposition transcriptsOnce a lawsuit is filedDoes the fee percentage also step up at filing?

When you may not need a lawyer

If you were barely hurt, fault is clear and the insurer is paying your bike damage and medical bills, you may be able to settle directly or use a short paid review instead of a contingency agreement. If you were hospitalized, are still treating, the insurer blames you, or the driver's coverage looks too small, talk to more than one lawyer; first consultations are often free (see consultation fees).

Rider checklist before you sign

  • Get the percentage at each stage in writing, and the exact event that triggers a step-up (filing suit, a set number of days before trial, appeal).
  • Ask whether the fee is calculated on the gross or after costs, and who pays costs if you lose.[1]
  • Ask whether the fee applies to your own UM/UIM, med-pay or property-damage claim, which may be paid with little dispute.
  • Ask who handles the motorcycle property-damage claim and whether that is free.
  • Preserve the bike, helmet and gear, and do not repair or sell the bike until your lawyer says it has been inspected.
  • Check your filing deadline; it is set by state law and varies (see your state page).

faq.q: Do motorcycle accident lawyers charge more than car accident lawyers?
faq.a: Usually the percentage is the same; what tends to be higher is the case cost, because fault is more often disputed and injuries are more serious. Compare written agreements from more than one firm rather than assuming a rider premium.

faq.q: Can I still recover if I was not wearing a helmet?
faq.a: Often yes, but it depends on your state's helmet law and fault rules and on whether the injury is one a helmet would have affected. Defendants may argue it reduced damages, which can add expert costs.

faq.q: Does the lawyer take a percentage of my own insurance claim?
faq.a: Only if the agreement says so. Ask whether the fee covers uninsured/underinsured motorist claims, med-pay and property damage, and at what rate, before you sign.

faq.q: What if I was partly at fault?
faq.a: Many states reduce damages by your share of fault and some bar recovery past a threshold. The fee is still a percentage of whatever is actually recovered after that reduction.
